title: Authentication, security, and privacy
summary: Separate identity from permission, validate every input, protect cookies and secrets, reduce attacks, and respect personal-data lifecycle.

lessons.title: Authentication, authorization, and permissions
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of the access decision for an action in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of the access decision for an action.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Authentication answers who are you; authorization answers may you do this specific thing to this resource. A valid session therefore does not automatically grant admin status; every sensitive mutation verifies minimal permission near the operation. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: the access decision for an action is like an airport where passport, ticket, baggage screening, and retention rules answer four different questions. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

401 means missing identity or invalid session, while 403 means known identity with insufficient rights; the distinction improves UX, logs, and audit. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

A permission names a resource and capability such as orders.refund; roles group permissions, but the route checks the effective capability. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

Least privilege gives every staff member only what the task needs and removes access promptly when responsibilities change. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Server validation and threat modeling
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of validation at an untrusted boundary in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of validation at an untrusted boundary.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Anything crossing URL, JSON, form, cookie, webhook, or file is controlled by another actor and arrives as unknown. Validation checks type, shape, length, bounds, and allowlists before domain logic; output encoding then protects each destination context. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: validation at an untrusted boundary is like an airport where passport, ticket, baggage screening, and retention rules answer four different questions. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

React escapes rendered text, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML or external HTML requires appropriate sanitization; storing a string does not make it safe for every context. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

Parameterized queries and SDKs prevent SQL injection; concatenating user filters into SQL restores risk despite superficial validation. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

CSRF concerns automatic cookies, SSRF URLs fetched by the server, and uploads disguised content; each needs a specific defense and limits. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

A decision that an identified actor may perform a specific action.
An action forced from another site using the victim’s cookies.

blocks.text: Defense in depth stacks independent barriers: JavaScript-inaccessible cookies, HTTPS transport, same-site policy, browser headers, server secrets, and rate limits. No barrier replaces validation and authorization, but each reduces the impact of a mistake. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: reduction of attack surface is like an airport where passport, ticket, baggage screening, and retention rules answer four different questions. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

HttpOnly reduces theft through XSS, Secure enforces HTTPS, SameSite limits some cross-site requests, maxAge bounds the session, and a signature detects tampering. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

NEXT_PUBLIC means public; after a leak, removing the string from the repository is insufficient: revoke, rotate, audit usage, and clean history if required. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

CSP, nosniff, frame-ancestors, and Referrer-Policy constrain the browser; rate limiting targets identity/IP/action with a window and 429 response without blocking the whole site. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Privacy and the data lifecycle
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of personal-data minimization in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of personal-data minimization.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Personal data follows a lifecycle: stated purpose, legal basis, minimal collection, limited access, defined retention, then deletion or anonymization. Consent is valid only when freely given, specific, informed, reversible, and as easy to refuse as accept. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: personal-data minimization is like an airport where passport, ticket, baggage screening, and retention rules answer four different questions. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

Strictly necessary cookies may support session or cart under the applicable framework; analytics and marketing load only after an explicit versioned choice. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

Refusal does not degrade essential features, withdrawal stops future collection, and identifiers controlled by the application are removed. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

A policy names data, purposes, recipients, retention, and rights; real export/deletion processes must match published text and backups. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
